name: DRI
seoDesc: DRI: work out weight from the BMI and the total daily calorie requirement. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The DRI calculator turns the BMI and the total daily calorie requirement into weight. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the DRI calculator work?
sections.html:
The DRI calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports weight in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex, the possible pregnancy and the age); then you type in the BMI and the total daily calorie requirement.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Sex: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Possible pregnancy: pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as not pregnant or lactating, pregnant and lactating. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Age: pick the option that matches your case — 9 options, such as birth to 6 months, 7–12 months and 1–3 years. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • BMI: a plain number with no unit attached.
  • Activity factor: pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as little/no exercise, exercise 1-2 times/week and exercise 2-3 times/week. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Total daily calorie requirement: a number, expressed in kcal/day.
  • Smoker: a single on/off switch — tick it for “Smoker”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

5 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the DRI calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Weight=(1 ÷ 40) × (activity factor × (20 × age − 25 × height + 664 × sex − 20) + 4 × total daily calorie requirement − 4 × possible pregnancy × sex) ÷ activity factor
Weight=(1 ÷ 10000) × BMI × (height ^ 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Weight: shown in kilograms, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Height: shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Height: Length, opening in centimeters
  • Weight: Mass, opening in kilograms

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The DRI calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the BMI and the total daily calorie requirement — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the DRI calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns weight, derived from the BMI and the total daily calorie requirement. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the DRI calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the BMI and the total daily calorie requirement, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the DRI calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
